# Data dependence

This page says, for each component and feature, whether it needs **stored customer data**. It also
says what each one does at three storage levels: off, metadata only, and everything.

## Summary

- **The rule:** a component or feature works from **metadata** only. A feature that needs
  **content** is a rare, deliberate exception. Many users turn storage off, and a feature that
  quietly needs content then works worse, with nothing reported.
- **12 of 23 components need no stored content to do their job:**
  - 4 keep nothing.
  - 2 keep only hashes or names: `cacheinject` keeps hashes, and `toolfilter` keeps tool names when
    tool deferral is on (the `ultrahigh` preset, or the Bob plugin's `bob-ultrahigh`).
  - 1 keeps only a speed-up cache.
  - 5 keep only the original. Without it they still work, but the `expand` tool cannot give it back.
- **5 more could work on metadata only**, with a small change: one "already done" flag per message.
- **4 components cannot work without content.** A model writes their text, and the words differ
  each time. These are `extract_llm`, `summarize`, `cache_aware_summarizer` and `agentdiet`.
- **2 are special cases.** `skeleton` refuses to run without storage. `extract_llm_sweep` holds only
  metadata (ids, hashes, counts, verdicts), but it keeps copies of the conversation in memory and
  its question to the model needs last turn's text.
- **Context Guru keeps content after the user opts out**, in 7 places. The worst are 2 full
  request bodies per thread, and the last request body for keep-alive.
- **With storage off today, use preset `conservative` and cache strategy `none` or `1-hour-head`.**
  Every other plugin preset pays for savings that last one turn, so it does not work.
- **"Metadata only" does not exist yet.** Today the Store keeps everything or nothing.

## Terms

- **Content**: text from the user or the agent, or text made from it. Examples: transcript text,
  tool output, request bodies, system prompts, tool declarations. A summary, a shortened tool
  output and a code skeleton are content too.
- **Metadata**: values that do not let you read the content back. Examples: hashes, counts,
  sizes, ids, token numbers, timestamps, flags. **A short hash of content is metadata.** A
  shortened copy, a sample, or the first characters of content are content.
- **Kept**: held after the request ends, in memory or on disk. Text held only while one request
  runs is not kept.
- **Store**: Context Guru's in-memory key-value store for each conversation. It is never written to
  disk. `store.enabled: false` replaces it with a Store that keeps nothing.
- **Original**: the text of a tool output before a component shortened it. Context Guru keeps it in
  the Store so the model can get it back with the `expand` tool.
- **Frozen decision**: the exact shortened text a component sent. Context Guru keeps it in the Store
  and sends the same text on every later turn.
- **Breaks the cache**: the next turn sends different bytes for a message the provider already
  cached. The user then pays to write the cache again, from that message to the end.
- **No way back**: the model cannot get removed text back through the `expand` tool. The agent
  still has its own copy.
- **Host**: the program that runs Context Guru. That is the proxy binary, or another program
  that uses Context Guru as a library. The host sends requests to the provider and holds
  credentials.
- **Kind** (in the tables): `none` (keeps nothing), `metadata`, or `content`. It is what the
  component keeps at the "Everything" level.
- **Decided by**: the person, and the issue or PR, that decided the current behaviour. If no later
  decision exists, it is the author of the PR that added the component. Ask that person before
  you change the row.

## The three storage levels

| Level | What Context Guru keeps | Exists today? |
|---|---|---|
| **Off** | Nothing in the Store. It keeps only the in-memory trackers that every request needs: how much of the conversation the provider cached, and when. These hold counts and timestamps. | **Partly.** `store.enabled: false` removes the Store. It does **not** remove the in-memory content in [Features outside the pipeline](#features-outside-the-pipeline). |
| **Metadata only** | Hashes, counts, ids, token numbers, timestamps and flags, in the Store and in memory. No content. | **No.** The "Metadata only" columns say what the code would do with a Store that refuses content. [What "metadata only" would need](#what-metadata-only-would-need) lists the changes. |
| **Everything** | Content and metadata. | Yes. This is the default. |

## Why Context Guru stores rewrites at all

The client never sees the rewritten request, so it cannot keep it.

1. The client (for example Claude Code) sends its **whole transcript** on every request.
2. Context Guru rewrites that copy and sends the result to the provider.
3. The provider returns **only the new assistant message**. The API cannot hand an edited history
   back.
4. The client **adds** that message to its own transcript. Its transcript still holds the
   original tool outputs.
5. On the next turn the client sends the originals again. Context Guru must make the same rewrite
   again.

The results:

- **A rewrite that depends only on the message needs no storage.** Context Guru runs it again every
  turn and gets the same bytes. Only CPU time is repeated. These components work this way:
  `format`, `toon`, `searchfold`, `textclean`, `toolfilter`, `cmdfilter`, `linecap`,
  `dedup`, `smartcrush` and `extract`.
- **Storage is necessary only when Context Guru cannot rebuild the rewrite from the message:**
  - **Model-written text** (`extract_llm`, `summarize`, `cache_aware_summarizer`, `agentdiet`). A
    model gives different words each time.
  - **Gated rewrites** (`mask`, `failed_run`, `collapse`, `readlifecycle`, `coref`). They act only
    on the part of the conversation that is not cached yet. On the next turn they must know that
    they already acted. A flag is enough.
- **The originals for `expand`** are a copy of what the client already has. Context Guru keeps them
  only because it cannot ask the client for its copy.

**Where the data sits matters.** Context Guru runs inside a host: the proxy binary, or another
program that uses it as a library. With the local plugin install, the Store is in the proxy process
on the user's own machine. That machine already holds the full transcript. Storing content is
mainly a question for the hosted service, where the Store is on our side.

**A possible change, not checked:** a plugin inside the client could rewrite the local transcript
itself. The client would then keep the shortened version, and Context Guru would not need to store
it. Nobody has checked if Claude Code's plugin or hook interface lets a plugin change earlier
messages.

## Will my setup work?

Find your preset and your cache strategy below. Each cell says what happens at that storage level.

- ✅ **Works**: the same as with everything stored.
- ✅ **Works, no `expand`**: the same savings. The model cannot ask for removed text back. The
  agent still has its own copy.
- 🟡 **Works, metadata**: it works, and it keeps **only metadata** to do it (hashes, counts,
  timestamps). It keeps no content.
- ❌ **Does not work**: it does nothing, or it pays for something that lasts only one turn. That
  is a model call, or a cache write when a shortened message comes back in full the next turn.
  The cell says which.

There is no "partly". A setup that pays for a saving that lasts one turn does not work.

"Metadata only" does not exist yet. That column says what would happen if it were added to the
code as it is today.

### Cache strategies

| Strategy | Off | Metadata only | Everything | Decided by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `none` | ✅ Works | ✅ Works | ✅ Works | David Amid, #569 |
| `auto` (was `5-min-ping`; `5-min-ping` is now an alias) | ❌ **Cannot work without storage.** A ping sends your last request again, so Context Guru must keep it. **Today it runs anyway and keeps it.** That breaks the opt-out (see [What this audit found](#what-this-audit-found)). | ❌ Cannot work, for the same reason | ✅ Works | David Amid, #569 |
| `1-ping`, `2-ping`, `30-min-ping` (the same ping mechanism as `auto`; they differ only in how many pings and when) | ❌ The same as `auto` | ❌ The same as `auto` | ✅ Works | David Amid, #569 |
| `1-hour-on-wait` (#1243, main agent only) | ❌ The same as `auto`: the ping needs the stored last request. | ❌ The same as `auto` | ✅ Works | David Amid, #1261, confirmed 2026-11-22 |
| `1-hour-always` (#1261, opt-in, main agent only) | ❌ The same as `auto` for subagent pings. The main thread gets no ping. The relabel reads metadata only: whether the body declares tools, the thread id, the model name and the usage counts. | ❌ The same as `auto` | ✅ Works | David Amid, #1261, confirmed 2026-11-22 |
| `1-hour-head` | ✅ Works. It sends no request of its own. It changes only a label on the request the client is sending, so the provider keeps that cache for 1 hour. It keeps nothing. | ✅ Works | ✅ Works | David Amid, #569 |

The named strategies are one table in the proxy (`config/strategy.go`, #980). That change only gives
the existing strategies one home and a `cache.strategy` key. It does not change what any strategy
keeps.

**Why `auto` (and the other ping strategies) needs storage and `1-hour-head` does not:** a ping is a **new** request that
Context Guru sends by itself while the user is idle. To read the same cache, the ping must have the
exact bytes of the last prompt, so Context Guru keeps them. `1-hour-head` only changes the request
that the client sends anyway. `1-hour-on-wait` (main agent only) relabels the markers of the keep-alive ping body only, never a real request. It reads metadata for its decision: the wait cause, the thread id, the model name, the client-compaction verdict, the fork or inherit flag, and the usage counts of the ping and of the thread's return. On a route where the switch is costly it also relabels the markers of every real request of a main thread to 1 hour, from its first big cold rebuild; the opt-in `1-hour-always` does so from the first request. Both read whether the body declares tools, the thread id and the prefix token counts, not the text. It keeps, in memory only, a small record per provider, endpoint, route and model (whether the grant is proven or off, and the deadline of the probe), and a record per thread for its pending probe (the route, the model, the time of the ping, and the prefix token count), and an index per thread of its last free 1-hour ping (the thread, the route, the alias and the store), until its next request or an hour from the ping. The tier and the time of that ping are the store's `cg:seen:` record (metadata: a time, a tier, a hash of the route and a request number), the one record of the fact, read by the cold check and the cache clock alike. When storage is off (no store keeps anything), the index also holds the ping time itself, as it did before, so the clock and the manual-ping refusal answer as they always did, and the cold check counts the ping's hour from it (`apply.Opts.FreePing`). It is the same metadata (a thread, a route, a time), in memory only. It also keeps, per main thread, one flag (in the 1-hour mode or not) and the time, entry lifetime and prefix token count of its last touch, in memory only. The cache clock of the band and the status line reads that record (`ttl_s` 3600, `ttl_unproven` and `free_hour_ping` in `/api/cachestate`). While that record is live, the band hides the Ping button and the proxy refuses a manual ping, because a press would move the entry back to 5 minutes. All of it is metadata. It stores no text. The client supplies the bytes, so Context Guru keeps nothing.

**The credential:** Context Guru itself does not keep it. It keeps only a handle, and the host that
runs it (for example the proxy binary) sends the ping through its Dispatcher. The proxy binary's
Dispatcher keeps the credential in memory, masked, until the hold ends.

`medium` makes its summary in the idle time that `auto` keeps warm. Without a ping strategy,
`medium` almost never makes a summary, at any level.

| `extract_llm_sweep` | content | Store: one **held answer** per thread (pinned, `cg:swh:`): for each judged output its tool-use id, a short hash of the message, its token counts, the model's keep-or-drop verdict, the length of the conversation when asked, the model name, the cost, and the wait cause. No text. Memory, not the Store: **two full copies of the conversation per thread** (the request as the pipeline holds it, and as the agent sent it), kept for a thread the keep-alive can ping, for at most 30 minutes, or, with `warm: true`, for a thread it cannot ping only while a warm question is due or running (#1191; at most 300 seconds after the request), for at most 256 threads. It writes **no** removals (`cg:res:`) any more. **Since the cold apply (#404 PR C), it also keeps, per applied drop, the original output** (the stash behind the `<<cg:HASH>>` marker, which is content, the same as every other offloader), and **metadata only** besides: a drop record per thread and output (`cg:swd:`: tool-use id, content key, marker id, token count, time, the kind, and **4-byte hashes of up to 48 identifiers** the output introduced, used to see a later reference), a marker-to-drop map (`cg:swx:`), and a process-wide counter ledger for the false-drop rate. No output text is in any record. **With `warm: true` (#491, off by default; on only in the Bob plugin's `bob-ultrahigh`)** it also keeps, **in memory only and never in the Store**: one waiting answer per thread (ids, hashes, counts, verdicts: metadata), for at most 30 minutes, **which also holds the drop verdicts a refused answer left behind (the same fields, at most 256 per thread, none older than 30 minutes since the question that judged them)**, and per thread a few numbers (the warm run length, the previous request's local token size, the cache read the provider reported for the previous turn (#1191: on a route with an unknown cache phase, such as IBM Bob's, a read above 0 makes the cache count as live on the next request, for the warm path, the apply of a held answer and the shadow report), the request count since the last question, a last-touched time, and a flag with the time a question is pending, 5 minutes at most), for at most 256 threads. The warm question uses the ping registry's existing conversation copy (already counted above) and keeps **no copy of its own**. Since #1191, with `warm: true` that registry copy is also kept for a thread the keep-alive cannot ping, such as IBM Bob's route, so the warm question can ask there. Such a copy is kept only while the warm question is due or running, only the warm question reads it (a ping never does), and it is dropped when the question ends or the request fails. An applied warm drop writes the same records and stash as a cold drop. **With sweep v3 (`selector: rule` or `hybrid`, or any v3 setting; off by default, needs `warm: true`)** the rules read tool names, tool input paths and commands from the request in flight, to see a file read that was read or written again, and a build, test or lint run that ran again. They write nothing new: no path or command is stored. Per thread they keep, in memory only, two numbers and two flags (the billed size after the last accepted cut, and whether a cut or a question is waiting). The counters hold counts and ratios only. **Rule (c), `rule_unreferenced` (off by default)** reads the text of later messages in the request in flight, to see whether any of them reuses an identifier the output introduced. This is the same reading the recheck already does for `referenced_later`, and it also stores nothing. The drop record gains the **name of the rule** (or `judge`) that chose the drop, a label with no content, so an expand can be counted per rule. Since #1191 the same label is also a count on the dashboard row of the request: the drops per rule (`sweep_v3_dropped_<rule>`) and the first expands per rule (`sweep_v3_expanded_<rule>`), counts only. **Since #1196** each request also counts its cache verdict once, by reason (`sweep_cache_verdict_<reason>`: `known_cold`, `known_warm`, `unknown_prefix`, `unknown_live`, `unknown_cold`), a count and nothing else. **With sweep v3 on, the drop record also gains the tool name and a hash of the file path or command of the call** that produced the output (an 8-byte hash, with a prefix that keeps a path and a command apart). **The path or command itself is not stored.** On each later request the sweep hashes the path or command of every later tool call and compares it with those hashes, to count a re-read of what a drop removed. The calls it hashes are read in flight, the same request text the rules already read. **With `tier_target` (#1329, off by default; needs sweep v3)** the sweep also reads the billed prompt size, the price table's tier lines and rates, and the growth per turn. These are token counts and prices. It stores nothing new and needs no customer text, so its data dependence does not change. **Since #721** the candidate scan and the cold apply also check whether a `<<cg:HASH>>` in an output has a Store key (presence only, no content read), so an output that merely quotes marker text is still a candidate. | ❌ **Does nothing.** It asks only at a keep-alive ping or, with `warm: true`, after a forwarded request, and both need the body stash. With no Store, the held answer is not kept. It costs nothing and removes nothing. | ✅ **Works for what it does today**: the held answer is metadata, so it is kept and rechecked. **But** the in-memory conversation copies are content, so this level is not metadata only in full (see the memory column). | ✅ Works: the question at the ping, the held answer, the recheck, shadow mode and the cold apply. The removals need the stash for `expand`. | It asks the agent's model which old outputs are spent, at the keep-alive ping, and keeps the answer until a cold request. The answer is ids, hashes, counts and verdicts, so it is metadata. The question needs the exact text from last turn, and the recheck needs the conversation the answer was given for, so it keeps copies of the conversation in memory. | David Amid, #118; ping-time question and held answer approved 2026-10-25 (#508); cold apply approved 2026-10-25 (#695); warm path approved 2026-10-26 (#491); sweep v3 rules reading tool names, paths and commands in flight approved 2026-10-28 (#491); the stored path hash (a hash of the file path or command in the drop record, never the path) approved 2026-11-01 (#491); the previous turn's cache read and the verdict counter: approved by David Amid 2026-11-22 (#1196); warm-on keeps the copy without a ping: approved 2026-11-26 (#1193) |
| `summarize` | content | Store: the model-written summary and the replaced turns. Memory: a copy of the turns while the model call runs. | ❌ **Does not work.** **Does not start** by default, because it cannot tell how full the window is. Without a session (`/compact`) it works in one request. No way back. | ❌ **Does not work.** **Pays for a summary every turn above 90% full, and throws it away.** The next turn can wait up to 120 seconds for it. **Cannot work.** | ✅ Works | It replaces old turns with a model-written summary, and the words differ each time. It must keep the summary to send the same bytes next turn. | Osher Elhadad, commit 68e8b51; checkpoint in #430 |
| `cache_aware_summarizer` | content | Store: the summary and the replaced turns. Memory: copies of turns, for summaries during idle time, after a cold turn, and for one request's lifetime while a summary waits for that request's body to be stashed (#722). | ❌ **Does not work.** **Does not start** by default, because it cannot tell how full the window is. | ❌ **Does not work.** It keeps copies of turns in memory, which is content. On Anthropic it does nothing and costs nothing. On OpenAI it **pays and throws the summary away** every turn. **Cannot work.** | ✅ Works | Like `summarize`, it must keep the summary to send the same bytes later. It also keeps the conversation in memory, to summarize while the user is idle. | Itay Nakash, #256 |
| `agentdiet` | content | Store: the frozen decision and the original step | ❌ **Does not work.** **Pays one model call per turn.** The step it shortened last turn comes back in full, which **breaks the cache**. | ❌ **Does not work**: the same as Off. **Cannot work.** | ✅ Works | A model rewrites one older agent step each turn, and the words differ each time. The history stays short only if Context Guru keeps every rewrite. | Itay Nakash, #66 |

### Libraries that are not components

- **`dsl`** (the filter engine) keeps nothing per request. It holds only the rules from your filter
  files. `cmdfilter` and `linecap` use it, and those two keep the originals.

## Features outside the pipeline

One file for each row: `docs/data-dependence/features/<slug>.md`.

| Feature | Kind | Off | Metadata only | Everything | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `expand` and the originals | content | ❌ Not offered. Removals have no way back. | ❌ Not offered | ✅ Works | When Context Guru replaces a large output with a short marker, it must keep the original. Otherwise it has nothing to give back. This now includes the agent's own summary request (Claude Code auto-compact and `/compact`). Context Guru used to forward that request untouched, so it kept nothing from it. It now shortens the history like any other turn, so the summary can carry a marker, and a marker needs the stored original to be expanded later. A summary request over 32 MiB is still forwarded untouched and keeps nothing. |
| Frozen decisions and saved model results | content | ❌ Gone | ❌ Gone. The rule-based components can use a flag instead. | ✅ Works. Kept for about 2.8 hours in memory. **With the dashboard on (`--session-state`, on by default): kept 24 hours in memory and also written to the dashboard database, then loaded back when the session returns.** | After Context Guru shortens a cached message, it must send the same text every later turn. Otherwise the user pays to write the cache again. |
| Billed-token and cache-time records | metadata | ❌ Gone. `summarize` cannot tell how full the window is. A warm cache can look cold when one conversation comes under two ids. | 🟡 Works, metadata. This record also makes `summarize` start, and so start to waste calls. | 🟡 Works, metadata | To know how full the window is, Context Guru needs the size the provider billed last turn. It also needs the time the cache was last used. The billed size is kept per session and per thread (one integer each). The per-thread one lets `coref` measure how fast one thread grows. Since #1183 it also decides the window-fraction size gate (`summarize`, `cache_aware_summarizer`, `coref`, `extract_llm`), so a small subagent no longer reads the main thread's size. Bob's model route also reports its cache writes, and the 1-hour part of them, in its OpenAI-style usage block. Only that route reads these counts. They are metadata, so this works the same at every storage level. Bob's model route has at least 2 backends that count tokens differently, so on that route only, the proxy also writes a backend label on each request row (`backend`: `A`, `B`, `other` or empty) and counts the labels in `/stats` (`bob_backend`). It makes the label from whether the reply id starts with `chatcmpl-`, from which field names the usage block has, and from the reply's model name (Bob's helper calls, `security` and `router`, get no label). It keeps only the label, never the id. When the label is `other`, it logs one warning per new kind of shape with the first 4 characters of the id, its length and 5 yes/no flags. The label is metadata, so it works the same at every storage level. With the dashboard off, only the `/stats` counts exist. |
| **Session state table** (`--session-state`, #769; on with `--dashboard`) | content and metadata | ❌ Off. Dashboard off, `--session-state=false`, or store off: nothing is written. Hosted: the same switches, so `--session-state=false` also leaves a hosted proxy with memory only. | 🟡 Works, metadata: only the keys of counts, hashes, ids and verdicts are written (`cg:bin:`, `cg:bint:`, `cg:len:`, `cg:ttl:`, `cg:seen:`, `cg:swd:`, `cg:swk:`, `cg:swx:`, `cg:rst:`, `cg:use:`, `cg:tdf:`, and since #1097 `cg:keep:`, the "keep in full" mark: a session id and a content hash, one byte of value, no content). Set `--session-state-metadata-only`. The table is in the dashboard database. Hosted (#1104): this level is the only one, always, whatever the flag says. It writes the same keys except `cg:swx:` (and `cg:xres:`): they carry no session id, only a content hash, so two tenants would share one row and a purge could not find it. Those two stay in memory, per tenant. Every other key starts with the tenant-scoped session id. | ✅ Works. **Also writes the content keys to the dashboard database**: the summary text (`cg:sum:`), `extract_llm` results (`cg:res:`, `cg:xres:`), freeze decisions (`cg:frz:`) and the sweep's held answer (`cg:swh:`). The rewind payloads (the stash) are never written. Hosted: not available. A hosted proxy never writes a content key for any tenant. | A restart, or a pause of more than 2.8 hours, deletes the summary checkpoint and the last billed input from memory. The next turn then sends the full transcript, which can be over the window, and the summary cannot start. A table lets the proxy give a returning session the same state it had. The same holds for the "keep in full" mark (#1097): after a restart, an output the agent expanded stays in full, so the warm cache is read, not rewritten. On a hosted proxy (#1104) the same table is in the dashboard database, **at metadata level only, always**: `--session-state-metadata-only` does not matter there, and no summary text or other content key is written for any tenant. Every key it writes starts with the tenant id, so one tenant never reads another's rows. The keys with no session id (`cg:swx:`, `cg:xres:`) are not written there at all. A hosted restart then gives a returning thread its metadata state back, like a local install. A config change that keeps the same components also copies the marks in memory from the old Store to the new one. The table is **not encrypted**. It has its own retention, not the dashboard's. A row lives 30 days after its last write. An eviction or an archive can end it earlier, when no other session uses its key. A host that erases a session can also end it now (`Memory.EraseSession`, for Cortex's session delete). The erase removes the session's rows from the table, from the writes not yet flushed, and from memory. It also removes from memory the session's "who stashed this" marks and each rewind payload that only that session stashed. The erase works the same at each level: it removes what that level wrote, so the data dependence does not change. Erasing every session (`Memory.EraseAll`) empties the table and memory. A hosted proxy refuses it, because the table belongs to every tenant. Decided by: David Amid, 2026-10-29; for the hosted table, David Amid, 2026-11-12 (#1104) (the dashboard database, on with the dashboard). David Amid confirmed the data-dependence change for `extract_llm_sweep`. Rows to confirm: `cache_aware_summarizer`, `summarize` (Itay Nakash). |
| **Tool deferral history** (`ultrahigh`, #485) | metadata | ❌ Off with no durable place: no dashboard database and tool deferral's own file cannot be opened. Then it lives in memory only, a restart starts it from zero, and nothing is deferred until 3 new sessions. With the Store off nothing is deferred at all. | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | To defer only the tools a user does not use, it keeps, per user, session and tool: whether the session declared the tool, whether it used or loaded it, the project folder and the time. The rule groups MCP tools by server (`mcp__<server>__*`) when it reads this; the table still holds tool names only. It keeps the newest 64 sessions per user, plus the newest 10 sessions of each project, up to 256 sessions per user in all. The extra sessions are there because the rule checks whether this project used a tool in its last 10 sessions; without them, a user in many projects would push a project's older sessions out, and the check would not see them. It deletes sessions idle longer than the session-state retention (30 days by default). The table is `tool_defer_history`, in the dashboard database when there is one, else in tool deferral's own file. A user's first deferral request copies that user's own sessions, and no other user's, from the dashboard's inventory tables. It also keeps the provider check result per endpoint, model and route (`tool_defer_probe`); that row describes an endpoint, not a user. An account purge deletes the user's history rows, thread records and opt-out flags. Tool names, ids, paths, flags and times only. Nothing is shared between users: the history, the records and the opt-outs are keyed by user, and the pending opt-outs are capped per user. The check spends the user's own credential, under $0.01 per check, once a day per model (a failed check is retried after 15 minutes). Decided by: David Amid, #485, 2026-11-02. |
| **Client compaction setting** (Claude Code #948; Bob and Codex #963) | metadata | ✅ Works. Nothing is kept: the proxy holds the setting in memory. | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | The user can move the point where Claude Code compacts its own transcript. The savings figures and the summarize trigger must use that point, or they are wrong for that user. The local proxy reads a few short setting values once, at start-up, from its env and from `settings.json` and `.claude.json` (Claude Code), `~/.bob/settings.json` (Bob) and `config.toml` (Codex), and holds them in memory. For Bob it also uses the client's own default threshold. For Bob, the local proxy also reads the model list that passes through it (`/inference/v1/model/info`). It keeps one window number for each model id, in memory only, at most 512 entries, replaced on each fetch, and never written anywhere. It writes the resulting C (a number) and its source (`configured` or `client_default`) on each request row (`compaction_point`, `compaction_point_source`). No transcript text, no paths, no other settings. A hosted proxy reads and captures nothing. Decided by: David Amid, #948, #963. |
| **Keep-alive pings** | content. The host keeps the credential. | ❌ **Should be off. Today it is still on**, and keeps the last body. The proxy binary also keeps the credential. | ❌ Off | ✅ Works | To keep the prompt cache warm, the proxy sends the exact same prompt again with the user's credential. Without the text, it cannot ping. The Ping button (`POST /api/me/cache/ping`) uses the same body and key. With keep-alive off, a request that carries the header `x-context-guru-ping: 1` is still held, for the button only: no ping is sent for it, and the body and key are released 300 seconds after the last request on a 5-minute cache, or 59 minutes after it on a 1-hour cache (a press does not extend it), and one account holds at most 16 such threads. Without the header nothing is held. The install adds the header and tells the user. An older install (from before `--no-ping-header`) gets it at its next session start, with the same notice. Any other install without the header is never changed. It gets a one-time note instead. The cache-state answer also carries the time of the next planned ping (a number, metadata), so the mod can hide the button while a ping fires before the cache expires. The manual holds also export counts and byte sizes to `/metrics` (holds evicted by bytes or count, too-large refusals, a body-size histogram, bytes held per tenant) and write one log line with sizes when a tenant holds 2 bodies of 8 MiB or more. These are metadata only and work at every storage level. **No dashboard, single-tenant (#1457):** the proxy still holds the thread and pings, under the account's cache strategy. The credential lives in process memory only. It is never written to the dashboard database, a store, capture storage, a state file, a log or a metric, and it is dropped when the hold ends or the process stops. No ping rows are written, because there is no dashboard. A ping's spend still goes to the metrics counters (`llm_savings_*`, numbers only). A hosted proxy with no dashboard holds nothing and pings nothing, as before: it keeps other people's credentials, so it needs an audit record first. A library host (Cortex, bifrost) is not affected: its own dispatcher resolves the credential. Decided by: David Amid, 2026-11-26 (#1457). |
| **Body stash** | content | ❌ **Should be off. Today it is still on**, with 2 full bodies per thread. | ❌ Off. The sweep's question then cannot be asked, and `cache_aware_summarizer` stops. | ✅ Works | To ask the model a cheap question, Context Guru adds the question to the exact text it sent last turn. The provider already cached that text. The sweep keeps **2 more full copies of the conversation per thread**, outside the stash, for a thread the keep-alive can ping, or, with the sweep's `warm: true`, while a warm question is due on a thread it cannot ping (see `extract_llm_sweep` above). Since #1457 a single-tenant proxy with no dashboard also keeps these copies, in memory only, for the threads it can ping. A hosted proxy with no dashboard still keeps none. |
| Observe-mode store | content | ❌ **Should follow the level. Today it is still a real Store.** | It should follow the level | ✅ Works | Observe mode runs the pipeline later on a copy, to estimate savings. The copy should store only what the real run would store. |
| Dashboard database | content and metadata | ❌ Off | 🟡 Works, metadata: numbers, fixed codes, ids, and tool, MCP-server and skill names. **No** before/after text, summaries, declaration text, error text or rejection text. | ✅ Works. It keeps text only when content capture is on. | The dashboard shows what Context Guru removed and what your setup carries. Every number on it needs only counts and prices. Every request row comes from traffic the proxy saw itself. On a local install the dashboard also reads two things from your disk, and stores neither: the working folder recorded in Claude Code's session files, to group folders into projects for the project picker, and each installed skill's description from its `SKILL.md`. The keep-alive calculator and recommendation (#868) replay the per-wait ping plan from columns the proxy already writes for each request: stop reason, wait cause, thread id, cache tier and provider. They read no text. The adapt and save-more replay (#1298) reads the same wait cause from each stored row to set its prefix floor. It is one short label and no text. Tool deferral's net-saving panel (#869) adds nine count and price columns per request: tokens deferred, the names list's tokens, searches, dropped searches, tools loaded, wrong guesses, and the gross, net and cost dollars. All three come from one figure: the accountant library's figure for the deferral. The net is that figure. It prices the definitions left out, the price-line change and the names list from the request bodies, and the search turns (the search output, the second pass over the loaded definitions, and their cache write on the next request) from token counts. The gross is its saved side, and the cost is gross less net. A request the library did not price (an unpriced model, a held estimate) books no dollars. The search-turn token counts are numbers from the response usage and our own token weights: no text. The tool inventory also records the built-in tools Claude Code defers (by name, with 0 tokens) and counts a tool loaded through search as a use. `save-more tools` reads the same inventory, the tool deferral history and the account's keep and always-defer lists. All of it is tool names, counts and prices, and works at the metadata level. Each request row also has one flag, `acc_priced` (context-guru#912), set when the accountant library priced the request. The keep-alive views read it to trust the library's stored rescue figure. It is a yes or no, with no text. Two more flags and two numbers sit beside it: `estimate_held` (a yes or no: the request's estimated figure was kept out of the totals), `estimated_saved_usd` (that figure, in dollars, the most it could be) and `estimated_saved_low_usd` (the least it could be). They hold no text. One more column, `acc_fallback` (#1004), holds a fixed code: why the accountant library could not price the request (`unpriced`, `unsupported_wire` and the like), or empty. The Overview counts these requests and leaves their cost out of the saving share. It holds no text. A request booked at $0 because the price list had not loaded is priced later from its own token counts and the model name, with no text (#920). Its compaction calls are priced the same way, from their model name and token counts, which the proxy keeps in memory and does not store (#1033). Each request row also keeps the unit of its costs, `currency` (`USD`, or a name the price file gives, such as `Bobcoins`): it is configuration from the price file, not user data. An earlier history import copied whole request rows from those session files; it is removed, and its rows are deleted when the database opens. The cache state (`/api/cachestate`) and the manual ping estimate the size of a session's next request. They take the median of the `fresh_input` plus `cache_write` token counts of the model's last `NextInputWindow` billed requests in the session. It is a count from the stored rows. No text is read. The stored text of tool declarations and system prompts (when content capture is on) follows the request rows it came from (#689). Retention, a size trim, an archive move and an account purge remove it when the last declaration that names it goes. Text that another session or account still names stays. Text left over from before this rule is removed once, when the proxy starts. The level of data dependence does not change: this only sets when the text is deleted. |

| Archive | content and metadata | ❌ Off | 🟡 Works, metadata rows only | ✅ Works | It moves old conversations off the local disk. The database stays small, and you can still open old history. |
| Insights | metadata | ❌ Off (it needs the dashboard) | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | A cost report needs only counts, tool names and prices, not the text. |
| **Subscription headline** (dashboard Overview, #985) | metadata | ❌ Off (it needs the dashboard) | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | On a Claude subscription the Overview shows every saving in tokens, not dollars, and an estimate of the 5-hour limit share. It reads the auth kind and the latest rate-limit numbers the proxy kept for the account (#984), and the token counts by tier and the cost totals the dashboard already has (#998). Since #1023 the Sessions tab shows the same token counts per session, summed from the same stored numbers. Since #1042 and #1048 the Cache strategy tab and its tables show them too. It keeps nothing new. Decided by: David Amid, #985 (2026-11-09) and #998. |
| Thread tracker | metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | It tells the main agent from its subagents. It uses hashes to check if a new request continues an earlier one. Since #947 it also marks the first request after the main agent's own compaction. It finds the client's own compaction request in two ways (#1314). First, a mark that needs no text: the `x-context-guru-request-kind: compaction` header that the OpenCode and Pi plugins set, and Codex's own `x-codex-turn-metadata` (its `request_kind` field). This is metadata only. Second, a match on the opening of the client's summary prompt in the last turn only (Claude Code, Bob Shell, Codex, OpenCode and Pi), read from `messages` or from the Responses `input`. This reads the text of the last turn. It is a deliberate exception, the same as before, and it is the fallback for a client that sends no mark or a host that passes no headers. With storage off or at the metadata level, the mark still works and the phrase match still runs on the request in flight. Nothing is stored. The proxy sends the mark to the accountant library and stores it on the request row (`client_compaction`: `unknown` or empty), where the replay cap reads it. A request the tracker could not judge (no session id, no message list) stores no mark. It is one short label, with no text. Since #1310 it also reads four more request headers to name a subagent: Codex's `x-codex-parent-thread-id` and `thread-id`, and OpenCode's `x-opencode-parent-session-id` and `x-opencode-session-id`. They are ids. They carry no text. The level does not change. |
| **Where Context Guru's own model call goes** (`agent.ModelTarget`, IBM Bob) | metadata | ✅ Works. It keeps nothing. | ✅ Works | ✅ Works | A summary call and the sweep's question go to the model of the request's own route, with the caller's own key. The route's agent names only the path and the scheme of the auth header. Bob's agent names Bob's model path and `Apikey`. So on Bob's route these calls go to Bob's own server, which already has the conversation. Before, they went to a path that Bob does not serve, and they failed. The agent never sees the key, and it keeps nothing. Such a route never uses the operator's OpenAI key: with no key of its own, the request makes no model call. What each component sends and stores does not change: see its row above. Decided by: Vitaly Zabershinsky, #1074. |
| Session tracker | metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | It needs a stable label for each conversation. When the client sends none, it hashes the start of the conversation. The Bob IDE sends its task id in a request header (`X-Task-Id`), and only the Bob model route reads it. Codex sends its own session id in a request header (`session-id`), and only a caller that says it is Codex reads it. That keeps one Codex session whole after a compaction. That is metadata only, and it works at every storage level. |
| Cache tracker | metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | It must know how much of the conversation the provider already cached, so components never edit that part. After a restart it asks the dashboard (when on) for the time each thread's cached prefix was last refreshed — by its own last request or a keep-alive ping that read or wrote the cache and got a 2xx reply, under either session id the conversation uses (the row stores the content-derived alias id, a hash like the session id itself); timestamps and ids, metadata only — and treats a thread refreshed inside the request's cache lifetime as cached, not as new, until that thread's first request. Without the dashboard — and for a tenant running observe mode, whose rows carry no session id — it uses the proxy's start time instead. |
| Accountant savings (per-component figures from the accountant library) | metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata. It runs on every request with no dashboard too (#1451). It keeps its state in memory only, and the dashboard only stores and shows the result. | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | To price a saving it must know which part of the conversation a rewrite changed and whether the provider had that part cached. It reads each request once and keeps only a hash and a size for each part, plus the cache breakpoints. The text is dropped as soon as it is hashed, and the hashes are held in memory, one set per conversation thread, plus each thread's last set for the sibling check (SharedWarm). So a restart does not lose them, it also saves them to one file beside the dashboard database (`<dashboard-db>.accountant-state.json`, readable by its owner only), every minute and when it stops, and loads them again when it starts. The file holds hashes, sizes, positions, and the ids and names the state needs (session and thread ids, tool and component names, model names, times). It holds no message text. It also holds one proxy version number, and it is ignored when that number differs or when it is more than one hour old, except for the thinking counts below. It is not written when there is no dashboard: with no dashboard the state stays in memory and is lost at a restart, and nothing else is stored. It reads the tools and system sections the same way, as names, hashes and sizes, to report the envelope changes. On the OpenAI Responses wire it reads `instructions` as the system section and each `input` item as one part, with the same hash and size and nothing more. The result it writes to the dashboard is dollar amounts for each component, with their split by tier. Since #998 it also writes the same figures as token counts by tier (fresh input, cache read, 5-minute and 1-hour cache write), saved and caused: per component row, and per request for the keep-alive rescue, the cache split, the 1-hour head and the ended-change break. They are numbers only. `/api/stats` sums them in its `tokens` object. Since #1187 it also keeps the token count of each thinking block a model made, so that a block the client sends back is priced at its own count and not at a fixed price. From each response, JSON or stream, it reads the signature of each thinking block, the `data` string of each redacted thinking block, and the response's `thinking_tokens`. It keeps a 64-bit hash of each of those strings and a count, never the strings or any text. A response with no count, a count of 0, or more than 64 blocks is not kept. The table holds at most 20,000 blocks, the oldest go first, and one table serves all tenants: a key is the hash of a string that only the tenant who got it holds. It is saved in the same state file, and it is restored from a file up to 24 hours old, also when the rest of the state is too old or the accountant library refuses it. A file with another proxy version gives back nothing. It is read only on the chat routes, from Anthropic responses. Since #1451 it runs on every request, with or without the dashboard, and it reads the same things in each case: sizes, hashes, token counts and, in memory for the length of one request, the request body it hashes. With no dashboard it stores nothing new on disk. It gives each request's Result to the metrics counters (`llm_savings_*`, which carry numbers only) and it has a per-request dollar figure (numbers only) for tool deferral's `/stats` ledger to read in #1445. The tool deferral ledger reads that figure. It also reads the thinking signatures of Anthropic responses with no dashboard, as hashes and counts in memory, so a thinking block that the client sends back is priced right. Since #1457 and #1460 a keep-alive ping books through a path that needs no dashboard. Since #1457 a single-tenant proxy pings without the dashboard too, and books through this same path. Only a hosted proxy with no dashboard sends no ping (the audit-sink rule). A manual ping (the Ping button) works like a scheduled one. For each ping that billed something, the proxy keeps the ping's facts in memory only, for the thread's next real request: the time of the ping, its window id and a few token counts and flags, at most 4096 threads, one entry per thread, never saved to disk. The next real request takes them and credits the rescue. A manual ping with no next request in the window books its spend only. Its estimated saving (`manual_saved_usd`) is no longer booked: a row written before #1460 keeps its estimate, and a row after it holds 0. The ping's spend goes to the metrics counters (`llm_savings_*`). These are numbers only. No level changes what it does. Decided by: David Amid, #998 (the figure), #1451 (the figure with no dashboard), and #1457 and #1460 (ping savings with no dashboard, and for a manual ping), and #1457 again for pings with no dashboard (2026-11-26). |
| Wait-cause and lifecycle signals | metadata | ❌ Off (it needs the dashboard) | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | To tell why the agent paused, it reads the request once. It keeps only counts and ids. Since #857 it also reads the **tool name** of the last tool call, to tell that an agent has finished (`done`). The keep-alive then sends no pings for that thread. A tool name is metadata, and the rule works at every storage level. Since #858 the keep-alive also uses the **wait cause** (from the stop reason, the tool names and the open-task counts), whether the thread id starts with `a:`, the token count of the prefix and the time of day, to pick the ping count, to ignore a strategy's time windows for a wait that is not for a person, and to skip the sweep question during a tool wait. Since #1225 the turn's wait cause is also read from the request body while the request goes upstream, by a function that writes and stores nothing, so the keep-alive plans the turn at response time. The dashboard writer reuses that reading, so the body is normally read once (twice when the scan was not ready in time). It sends no body and no text to the keep-alive: only open-task counts. The body is already in memory during the request, and the level does not change. It also keeps one flag per thread: "has a tool call been seen". Since #1310 it also reads the **tool name** `request_user_input` (Codex's question tool), the marker text Codex puts in a terminal tool result (`Process running with session ID`, `Process exited with code`) and the client's User-Agent, to pick the cause when a turn ends with nothing open: `human` for Claude Code and Bob, `unknown` for any other client. The marker is a string match on the result, read only for the Codex client, as for Claude Code. All of it is metadata, and it works at every storage level. |
| **Next-request metadata** (#1198) | metadata | ❌ Off (it needs the dashboard). The proxy computes the values and keeps nothing. | 🟡 Works, metadata | 🟡 Works, metadata | To learn when the next request on a thread arrives and what wakes it (a person, a tool, a background task, a subagent, a teammate), the dashboard stores 14 small values on each request row and one small table of client signals. All of them are numbers, flags, fixed codes or a keyed hash. **None is text from the user or the agent.** A value that the proxy cannot work out is stored as empty (NULL), never as a guess. The values: (1) the **`timeout`** (a number) and **`run_in_background`** (a flag) of the tool call the thread waits for. The proxy reads only these two keys from the call's input. It never reads, stores or logs the rest of the input, such as the command. (2) A **prompt code** (`none`, `permission`, `question`, `other`), from the tool name `AskUserQuestion`, `ExitPlanMode` or `request_user_input` (Codex) and from the client's Notification signal. (3) The **client signals** the plugin hooks send (`SessionEnd` with its reason, `SessionStart` with its source, `Notification` with its type). The OpenCode plugin sends them too since #1313, from OpenCode's own events, with the same fields and only for a session it routed: the proxy stores the event name, the reason from a closed list, the time and the session id. It stores nothing else from the hook payload. (4) The **time zone offset** in minutes, from the proxy's own clock. A hosted proxy stores none. (5) The **turn number** of the thread, counted from the stored rows. (6) The **number of active threads** of the session in the last 10 minutes, counted from the stored rows. (7) The **keep-alive plan**: planned pings, the prefix floor and the idle seconds. These come from the configuration. (8) A **user hash**: the first 64 bits of an HMAC-SHA256 of the account id that Claude Code sends in `metadata.user_id` (the device id when the account id is empty), made with a random secret that the proxy keeps in a private file next to the dashboard database. **This is a pseudonymous id**: it is stable for one person on one install, and no one can turn it back into the account id without the secret. The raw id is never stored. A hosted proxy mixes the tenant into the hash, so one person in two tenants gets two hashes. (9) The **session mode**: how the client was started (`cli`, `headless`, `sdk`, `other`, from the User-Agent) and its permission mode (`default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `bypassPermissions`, `dontAsk`, `other`, from the hook input; the plugin sends only this one word). (10) The **subagent type** and **fan-out** of the subagent calls a response makes: a built-in name, or a keyed hash for a name the user chose, and a count. The prompt of the call is never read. The turn, the active threads and the signals are kept in the database, so they survive a restart. Retention and the database size cap delete the rows. The signals are also deleted with their tenant. |

## What "metadata only" would need

1. **A separate "may store content" check.** Every component must ask it before a model call, and
   Context Guru must ask it before it offers `expand`. Today one flag answers two questions: "can I
   keep the original?" and "can I keep the result?". Either answer makes some components pay for
   a model call and then throw the result away.
2. **An "already done" flag per message** for the rule-based components. All of them except
   `skeleton` can build the same text again from the message the client sends again. The flag
   keeps the cache stable. The code already has a path that builds lost text again; the flag
   would start it.
3. **Two small extra values:** the cut size for `collapse`, and the label for `readlifecycle`.
4. **A way for `coref` to send its cuts again.** Until then, turn `coref` off at this level.
5. **A byte bound, and a switch, for the sweep's in-memory conversation copies** (#404 PR C). The removals it used to repeat from a flag are gone: the sweep no longer writes them.
6. **Turn off the model-written components** (`extract_llm`, `summarize`, `cache_aware_summarizer`,
   `agentdiet`). Context Guru cannot build their text again, so they either pay for nothing or break
   the cache.
7. **Turn off** keep-alive, the body stash and `expand`. The dashboard keeps only metadata columns,
   and its memos keep only hashes and counts.

## What this audit found

The audit read the code at commit 2a7a86f. This page records the findings. It does not change any
behaviour. Each finding needs a decision from its owner.

### Content kept after the user opted out

1. **The body stash** keeps 2 full request bodies per thread, on every successful request. No
   switch turns it off. It fills even when no component uses it.
2. **Keep-alive** keeps the last request body, with storage off and with content capture off.
   The proxy binary's Dispatcher also keeps the user's credential, masked, for the same time. The
   plugin turns keep-alive on by default. See #595.
3. **Fixed by #689:** retention, size limits and an account purge now delete `declaration_text`
   when the last declaration that names it goes. Tool declarations and whole system prompts
   still stay after the user turns consent off, until retention or a purge removes them.
4. **Turning consent off deletes nothing.** Old rows in `request_content`, `extraction_calls` and
   the archive stay until retention or a purge removes them.
5. **The dashboard writes some columns without consent:** tool, MCP-server and skill names,
   `extraction_calls.rejection` (it can hold the provider's error text), and
   `request_components.err` (not scrubbed).
6. **Some in-memory copies ignore both switches:** the dashboard memos, the `toolschema` cache, the
   `cache_aware_summarizer` copies of turns, the `extract_llm_sweep` conversation copies (2 per
   thread, only where the keep-alive can ping), and the observe-mode store.
7. **In hosted mode, `--store` changes only the operator's config.** Each account follows only its
   own `store.enabled`.

### Problems with storage off today

- **7 components do not work.** They pay for a saving that lasts one turn: `mask`, `failed_run`,
  `collapse`, `readlifecycle`, `coref`, `extract_llm` and `agentdiet`.
  - Each one shortens a message once, then sends it in full the next turn. The user pays a cache
    write each time, so storage off can cost more than no compaction.
  - `extract_llm` and `agentdiet` also pay for a model call each time.
  - `coref` also loses its spending limit.
- **The summarizers do not work.**
  - `summarize` and `cache_aware_summarizer` do not start with their default settings. This is
    safe only by accident. They start as soon as Context Guru keeps the billed-token record, as at
    "metadata only".
  - `summarizer1509` starts at a fixed size, pays for a summary every turn and throws it away.
- **`skeleton` refuses to run.** This is the safe behaviour.
- **No way back** for the rest: `cmdfilter`, `linecap`, `dedup`, `smartcrush` and `extract` still
  work, but the model cannot get removed text back through `expand`.
- **Nothing warns at startup** when a component that does not work runs with storage off.

### Code comments that disagreed with the defaults

This PR fixes 3 code comments that said the wrong default:

- The dashboard's `CaptureContent` comment said "on by default". It is off.
- The account `CaptureContent` comment said "Off by default". A new account starts with it **on**.
- The `LifecycleSignals` comment said "Off by default". The flag is on by default. It writes only
  counts.

## Open questions

1. **Does "Off" allow in-memory metadata?** This page says yes. Without the cache tracker,
   components can edit the cached part of the conversation.
2. **Are tool, MCP-server and skill names metadata?** They are ids, but the user chooses them.
3. **Are content hashes metadata?** They are short SHA-256 values with no secret salt. A person who
   can read the Store can check if Context Guru saw a guessed text. A secret salt stops that.
4. **Is a session id from the client metadata?** It can contain a user or account id.

## Keep this page right

[`CLAUDE.md`](https://github.com/rossoctl/context-guru/blob/main/CLAUDE.md) holds the rule, under
"Hard boundaries". The PR template asks for it.

- Every PR that adds or changes a component or feature states its data dependence at each level.
  It also adds or edits the row file, and then runs `go run ./cmd/gen-datadep` (see
  [How to add or change a row](#how-to-add-or-change-a-row)).
- A PR that changes a row's **Kind** or a level column, in either direction, says so at the top.
  The person in "Decided by" confirms it before merge.
- Write the reason in plain words: **why** the component needs the data. A file name or line
  number is not a reason, and the test rejects it.

## How to add or change a row

This page is **generated**. Do not edit `docs/data-dependence.md` by hand.

1. Add or edit one file: `docs/data-dependence/components/<name>.md` for a pipeline component
   (the file name is the component name), or `docs/data-dependence/features/<slug>.md` for a
   feature. Copy a file that is next to it.
2. A row file has a front matter and a body. The front matter is `key: value`, one line for each
   key. It is not YAML. The body is the **Reason**, in plain words.
   - Component keys: `name`, `kind`, `where`, `off`, `metadata_only`, `everything`, `decided_by`.
   - Feature keys: `name`, `kind`, `off`, `metadata_only`, `everything`.
   - `order` (optional) is a number. Rows sort by `order`, then by file name. Without it, a row
     goes to the end, in file name order.
3. Run `go run ./cmd/gen-datadep` from the repo root. Commit the row file **and** this page.
4. `internal/datadep` has a test that fails when this page is not what the generator makes.
5. **A conflict in this page** after a merge or a rebase: take either side, and run
   `go run ./cmd/gen-datadep` again. Do not resolve it by hand. The row files do not conflict
   when two PRs touch different rows.

The text of this page outside the two tables is in `docs/data-dependence/page.md.tmpl`. Edit that
file for it, and run the generator.

## Technical notes: what each switch turns off

| Switch | Default | Turns off | Does not turn off |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store.enabled` (YAML) | on | The Store: originals, frozen decisions, saved model results, billed-token and cache-time records. Context Guru stops offering the `expand` tool. | The observe-mode store, the body stash, keep-alive bodies and credentials, component caches in memory, the dashboard |
| `--store` / `STORE` | follows YAML | Overrides the operator's `store.enabled` | In hosted mode, each account's own `store.enabled` |
| `--dashboard` / `DASHBOARD` | off (the plugin turns it on) | The dashboard database and its in-memory memos. In hosted mode, keep-alive also stops keeping bodies (a single-tenant proxy still keeps them, in memory). | The body stash, the Store |
| `--dashboard-content` / `DASHBOARD_CONTENT` | off | New writes of `request_content`, extraction-call text and `declaration_text` | Tool, MCP-server and skill names; `extraction_calls.rejection`; `request_components.err`; rows already written; keep-alive; the body stash; the memos |
| Account consent `capture_content` (hosted) | **on** for a new account | The same as `--dashboard-content`, for one account. Both must be on. | The same as the row above. Turning it off deletes nothing. |
| `--dashboard-retention` and size limits | 7 days, 512 MiB | Old dashboard rows, with their content | `tenant_spend`, `archived_sessions` |
| `--dashboard-backup` / `DASHBOARD_BACKUP` | on | The backup copies `<db>.bak` and `<db>.bak.1`. Before the age, size or quota rule deletes rows, the janitor copies the whole dashboard database (`VACUUM INTO`), content rows included, to that file (mode 0600, not encrypted). The copy before it moves to `<db>.bak.1`. A new copy is made only when the newest is older than 24 hours. Two copies at most, so **up to twice the database size on disk**. It holds the stored data at every storage level, so with `--dashboard-content` it holds the captured text. The disk-pressure rule makes no copy. An in-memory database has none. Decided by: David Amid, #1204, confirmed 2026-11-18. | The deletes themselves |
| `--archive-remote` | off | Upload of old sessions to remote storage | — |
| `cache.keepalive` (YAML), plugin strategy `none` | off in Go, `5-min-ping` in the plugin | Keep-alive bodies, the held credential, and pings | Manager strategies and per-session overrides can turn it on again |
| `CONTEXT_GURU_KEEPALIVE=off` | unset | All keep-alive, everywhere | — |
| `INJECT_EXPAND` | `auto` | The `expand` tool offer | Storing the originals |
| `CONTEXT_GURU_DUMP`, `CONTEXT_GURU_CAPTURE` | unset | (opt-in) Writes before/after text or whole request bodies to a file, with no redaction. Context Guru refuses them in hosted mode. | — |
| `CG_LOG_LEVEL=debug` | `info` | (opt-in) Logs the first 160 characters of each tool output | — |

The **body stash** keeps the last request body of each thread, for a cheap question to the model
(see [Features outside the pipeline](#features-outside-the-pipeline)). **No switch** turns it off.
